`cfb2nfl` studies what shapes a college football player's path to the NFL
draft, and how well we could have seen it coming from what we knew during their
career. This page is the short version; the full working plan lives in the
project's [VISION.md](https://github.com/ngiangre/cfb2nfl/blob/main/VISION.md).

## The questions

- What is it about a player's college career that actually predicts turning pro?
- Does the **head coach** matter (and later, coordinators, position coaches, and
  strength & conditioning staff)?
- After each season, what is a player's **percent chance of being drafted**,
  broken down by position?
- For the players who get drafted, what do they go on to do in the NFL — the
  statistics they put up, and **how long they last**?

Want to chase your own version of these? The **Explore** page lets you poke at
the data with interactive charts, and **Analysis** collects the write-ups as
they take shape.

## What we're looking at first

- **Coaching:** who the head coach is and how the program is doing (wins and a
  couple of standard team-strength ratings), plus whether the **head coach
  changed** from one season to the next.
- **Transfers:** whether a player switched schools, and whether that move was a
  step **up, sideways, or down** in level of competition (Power conference,
  Group of Five, or FCS-and-below) — measured season by season, since
  conferences shuffle over the years.
- **Size:** the player's height and weight from the team roster. (We hoped to
  track weight *changes* between seasons, but our source lists just one weight
  per player, so that isn't possible yet — see the Data page.)
- **Who we count and what counts as "made it":** every player with a college
  stat line, in the seasons they were eligible for the draft; the outcome we
  track is whether they were drafted.
- **What happens next:** for the players who get drafted, we now follow them into
  the NFL — **how long they last** (seasons on an NFL roster) and the statistics
  they put up, from [nflverse](https://nflverse.nflreadr.com/). This is an
  *outcome* we describe and forecast, kept separate from anything used to predict
  the draft itself.

## How we try to answer them

We go after every question two ways at once:

- **Why** — which things actually carry information about turning pro, and how
  sure we can be about each one.
- **How well we can call it** — whether we could genuinely have *predicted*
  future draft classes, not just explained the past after the fact.

The honest test is the second one. When we say a model can predict a draft
class, it's only allowed to use what we'd have known *before* that class was
picked — no peeking at the future. That's a much harder bar than fitting numbers
we already have, and it's the one we hold ourselves to.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For the stats-minded

This follows Breiman's *Two Cultures*, used side by side: **data models** for
explanation and inference, **algorithmic models** for prediction — with
**out-of-time validation** as the headline metric (a model predicting a draft
class only sees data through the prior season). Decisions are recorded in an
ADR-style **decision log**; logic is tested with `testthat` and data with
`pointblank` **contracts** that run inside the pipeline. The **Data** page has
the resulting provenance record and the **Pipeline** page has the processing
graph.
:::
